hook_text: Every waterfall on earth is slowly walking backwards, and it leaves a canyon in its footprints.
clip_script: Here's the secret of a waterfall. Hard rock on top. Soft rock underneath. The river crosses the hard rock and hits the soft rock, which wears away fast. A step forms. Water crashes down and drills a deep plunge pool. Spray eats away the soft rock behind the curtain of water. Now the hard rock is a shelf with nothing underneath. Crack. It collapses. The waterfall has moved backwards. Again and again, for thousands of years. Behind it lies a deep, narrow gorge, like the 18-kilometre gorge below Augrabies Falls. Give a river millions of years, and it can carve a canyon hundreds of metres deep, like the Blyde River Canyon or Namibia's Fish River Canyon. Waterfalls really do walk. Just very, very slowly.
visual_style: A cross-section diagram of hard and soft rock layers with water flowing; a plunge pool forming; an overhang cracking and falling; an aerial view of a gorge and a deep green canyon.
pacing: Step by step, with a pause before the overhang collapses.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn how waterfalls, rapids, gorges and canyons are formed.
